title: Reading crochet abbreviation tables
subtitle: How to decode and use the abbreviation list at the beginning of a crochet pattern
excerpt: Every crochet pattern uses abbreviations for stitch names and instructions. Patterns from different countries and publishers use different abbreviation systems, and some designers define their own non-standard abbreviations. The abbreviation table at the beginning of a pattern is the only reliable key to what the abbreviations in that particular pattern mean. Reading it before starting prevents the most common pattern-reading mistakes.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins). Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing).

glossaryTerms.definition: A short code used in a pattern to represent a stitch or instruction, such as dc for double crochet (UK) or sc for single crochet (US). Abbreviations vary between UK and US patterns and between publishers.

An instruction within a pattern that defines a non-standard stitch combination used only in that pattern, such as 'bobble = 5-tr cluster worked into the same stitch.' Special stitch definitions must be read before beginning the pattern.

content.text: Crochet abbreviations

are not universal. The abbreviation "dc" means double crochet in UK patterns and double crochet in US patterns, but UK double crochet and US double crochet are different stitches: UK dc = US sc; UK tr = US dc. Reading a UK pattern with US abbreviations assumed, or vice versa, produces a completely different fabric from the intended one. Always read the pattern's own abbreviation table first.
How to identify whether a pattern is UK or US
Check the pattern's stated terminology convention. Most patterns state "UK terminology" or "US terminology" near the top or in the abbreviation table.

If the pattern uses "sl st" (slip stitch) and "sc" (single crochet), it is almost certainly US terminology. If it uses "dc" to mean a fabric-building stitch with no "sc" at all, it is likely UK terminology.

Patterns from UK publishers (Stylecraft, King Cole, Rico, DMC UK, Rowan) are UK terminology. Patterns from US publishers (Lion Brand, Caron, Red Heart, Ravelry patterns from US designers) are US terminology.
Reading the pattern's abbreviation table
Read the full abbreviation list before picking up the hook. Look for any stitch you do not recognise and find its full definition in the table or in the special stitches section.
Check the
special stitch definitions

. These are the non-standard combinations the designer invented for this particular pattern and are not defined anywhere else. Missing a special stitch definition means you will not be able to work the pattern correctly.

Note any abbreviations that share a letter with a common stitch you know but with a different meaning in this pattern. For example, a pattern may define "dc" as a 3-tr bobble rather than double crochet. This is non-standard but does happen.

For each unfamiliar stitch, work a small test of the stitch on a scrap of yarn before starting the project. Discovering you cannot work a stitch mid-pattern is more disruptive than discovering it during preparation.
Common UK versus US stitch name conversions
UK double crochet (dc) = US single crochet (sc)
UK half treble (htr) = US half double crochet (hdc)
UK treble (tr) = US double crochet (dc)
UK double treble (dtr) = US treble crochet (tr)
Common problems

items.symptom: The stitch count per row does not match the pattern after the first row
items.cause: UK and US terminology was mixed: the abbreviation was read in the wrong convention.
items.fix: Re-read the pattern's terminology statement. If the pattern is US and you worked UK stitches (or vice versa), the stitch heights will be wrong, affecting every stitch count. Frog the work back and start again in the correct convention.

items.symptom: A special stitch is referenced in the main pattern instructions but not explained
items.cause: The special stitch definition was missed, or the pattern has an error and the definition was omitted.
items.fix: Search the pattern PDF for the stitch name. If it is absent from the pattern entirely, check the designer's errata, Ravelry forum, or contact the designer. Do not guess what the stitch is.

content.text: What to try next
Keep a reference card with the UK-to-US stitch name equivalents. Note which convention each pattern uses. Over time, checking the convention becomes automatic rather than a deliberate step.
